the microbiota of woodlarks and their sympatric skylarks share similar taxonomic composition, but are highly variable among individuals and among bird body parts.
the microbiota of sympatric species of birds are more similar than expected, suggesting that horizontal acquisition is a key factor for microbiota assembly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecological factors shaping the microbiota assembly in two sympatric bird species and provides new insight into the assembly of bird-associated microbiotas
the assembly of avian microbiota and the processes shaping the variation of microbial communities in different body niches.
the assembly of microbiotas in a natural setting, which is a key issue for the understanding of the ecological and evolutionary roles of the microbiota in animal life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the assembly of bird microbiotas is shaped by multiple factors, including phylogeny, environment, host behaviour and spatial heterogeneity, and that the relative importance of these factors varies among host body sites and among species.
bird-associated microbiota are shaped by a complex combination of intrinsic and extrinsic factors, and that the extent of niche-sharing is a key determinant of microbiota convergence.
the microbiota of woodlarks and of skylarks is similar, but not identical.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the microbial communities associated with the cloaca, skin and feathers of woodlarks and their sympatric skylarks are primarily shaped by environmental factors and to a lesser extent, by intrinsic factors.
bird-associated microbiota is primarily shaped by the regional bacterial pool, and that the extent of niche-sharing by hosts may predict the extent of microbiota convergence.

the microbial communities of woodlark and skylark are more similar than expected from their phylogenetic distance, and that the microbiota of these two species are primarily assembled from the local bacterial community pool, but that the extent of niche-sharing between individuals may influence the extent of convergence in their microbiota.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the study of avian microbiota should be expanded to encompass the whole breeding environment and include multiple body parts, as well as the comparison of closely related sympatric species.
, despite variation in microbiota composition, the two lark species harboured microbiota of similar composition, which suggests that the microbiota may be less variable than previously thought.
, in order to understand microbiota evolution and function, it is essential to characterise and compare microbiotas at multiple levels of biological organisation.
